title: Three Ways a Drug Moves a Receptor

scenes.tts: Does a receptor with an empty pocket stay silent? Not quite. A G protein coupled receptor is flexible. Even with nothing bound, it flickers between inactive and active shapes. For many receptors, a small fraction is active at any moment. So the receptor signals a little with no ligand at all. This is basal activity, and it gives a drug three ways to act.

scenes.visual: Four receptors (two bars crossing a membrane band, a cup at the top) sit with empty pockets beside an empty signal meter marked with a question mark. They flicker one at a time between a blue closed shape and a green splayed shape; the meter rises to a dashed basal line; a header names three ways to act.
scenes.narration: Does a receptor with an empty pocket stay silent? Not quite. A G-protein-coupled receptor is flexible. Even with nothing bound, it flickers between inactive and active shapes. For many receptors, a small fraction is active at any moment. So the receptor signals a little with no ligand at all. This is basal activity, and it gives a drug three ways to act.

scenes.tts: The first way is an agonist. It binds the active shape more tightly, so it holds receptors in that shape. Signaling rises above the basal level.
scenes.visual: Same stage at basal. A yellow ligand dot drops into the cup of the active receptor and stays; two more receptors flip to the green shape and take dots; the meter climbs above the dashed basal line.
scenes.narration: The first way is an agonist. It binds the active shape more tightly, so it holds receptors in that shape. Signaling rises above the basal level.

scenes.tts: The second is a neutral antagonist. It binds both shapes equally well. Alone, it changes nothing. But it occupies the pocket, so it keeps other ligands out.
scenes.visual: Same stage at basal. Purple dots enter one blue and one green receptor, then the rest; the meter does not move. A yellow agonist dot comes down to an occupied pocket and bounces back.
scenes.narration: The second is a neutral antagonist. It binds both shapes equally well. Alone, it changes nothing. But it occupies the pocket, so it keeps other ligands out.

scenes.tts: The third is an inverse agonist. It binds the inactive shape more tightly. So it pulls receptors out of the active state, and signaling falls below basal. In a cell with no basal activity, an antagonist and an inverse agonist look the same. You need a system with measurable basal activity to tell them apart. Many drugs long called antagonists proved to be inverse agonists when tested that way.
scenes.visual: Red dots enter the blue receptors, then the green one turns blue and the meter falls below the dashed line. A cell with no basal activity: all blue, meter at zero, purple-dotted and red-dotted pairs give the same empty meter. Basal returns; two tags sit at different levels. A purple 'long called antagonists' pill turns into a red 'inverse agonists when tested that way' pill.
scenes.narration: The third is an inverse agonist. It binds the inactive shape more tightly. So it pulls receptors out of the active state, and signaling falls below basal. In a cell with no basal activity, an antagonist and an inverse agonist look the same. You need a system with measurable basal activity to tell them apart. Many drugs long called antagonists proved to be inverse agonists when tested that way.
